opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one of the harder parts of the problem. Composition isn't something you can capture with a single scalar very easily, because it's not just "is the object there" or "does the image match the caption." It's about spatial relationships, balance, where the eye goes, how foreground and background interact, and whether the layout actually serves what the prompt is asking for.

So the way I think about it, the reward should be decomposed rather than monolithic. You want one component that checks semantic fidelity: are the right entities present, are the attributes bound to the right objects. Then a separate component that looks at structure: relative positions, counts, scale, occlusion, whether "the cup on the left of the laptop" actually ends up on the left. That part benefits a lot from grounding. You can use detection or segmentation signals so the reward is tied to verifiable spatial facts instead of a vague aesthetic judgment.

On top of that there's the more subjective, aesthetic layer: rule of thirds, visual balance, negative space, depth cues. I'd be careful there, because if you weight aesthetics too heavily the model learns a kind of generic "pretty photo" template and starts ignoring the prompt. We've seen that kind of reward hacking a lot, where everything drifts toward centered subjects with a blurry background because that scores well.

The other piece I care about is making the reward reasoning-aware. Instead of the critic just outputting a number, it should articulate why: "the second person is missing," "the lighting direction is inconsistent with the shadow." That gives you a denser, more interpretable signal, and it lets you assign credit to specific failures rather than penalizing the whole image uniformly.

And finally, composition should be weighted relative to the prompt. If someone asks for a minimalist product shot, the compositional expectations are very different from a crowded street scene. So I'd condition the reward on the intent of the prompt rather than applying a fixed notion of good composition everywhere. That adaptivity is, I think, where a lot of the remaining gains are.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly it's one of the harder parts of the whole setup. When we started thinking about the reward for R2, the temptation is to just plug in an aesthetic scorer or a CLIP-based preference model and call it a day. But those signals are mostly about local quality — sharpness, texture, whether the colors look pleasing. They don't really capture whether the image is well composed, whether the subject is placed with intention, whether there's balance between foreground and background, whether the negative space is doing any work.

So the way I think about it, composition has to be treated as a structural property, not a pixel-level property. That means the reward needs to see the image at a layout level. One thing that works reasonably well is to decompose the reward into components. You have a semantic fidelity term — does the image actually contain what the prompt asked for. You have a perceptual quality term. And then you add a term that looks at geometry: where are the salient regions, how are they distributed, does the arrangement match what a human would consider a deliberate frame rather than an accidental one. You can get that signal from saliency models, from object detectors giving you bounding boxes and their relative positions, or from a learned model trained on human preference pairs where the only thing varying is layout.

The subtle part is that composition is not one thing. Rule of thirds is a cliché, but there are plenty of great images that violate it on purpose. Centered symmetric compositions are powerful in some contexts and boring in others. So I'd be careful about hard-coding rules. What I'd rather do is let the reward be conditional on the prompt and on the intended style. If someone asks for a product shot, centered and clean is correct. If they ask for an editorial street photograph, you want more tension and asymmetry. The reward model should be reading that intent, not applying a single universal template.

The other thing I'd flag is reward hacking. If you make the composition term too explicit, the policy will find the cheapest way to satisfy it — put the subject at the one-third line and crop everything else out. So you need the term to be learned from human judgments, to be relatively smooth, and ideally to be combined with the other terms in a way that doesn't let one dominate. In practice we've found that a modest weight on composition, used mostly as a tie-breaker between candidates that already score well on fidelity, gives you noticeably better images without the model collapsing into a handful of layouts.

And then there's the question of where the signal comes from at all. A lot of the real gains, I think, come from pairwise human comparisons where annotators are shown two generations of the same prompt and asked which one is better framed. That's expensive, but it's much more informative than absolute scores, and it lets the reward learn the kind of taste that's hard to write down as a formula.

astra-6.text:
I think the reward should look at the image as a whole, because having all the right objects doesn’t necessarily mean you have a good composition. You also care about their relative positions, their scale, and the relationships between them. If the prompt asks for one object behind another, for example, the reward should capture whether that relationship is actually satisfied.

But composition is also subjective. A centered subject might work beautifully for one image, while an asymmetric arrangement works better for another. So I would avoid rewarding a single fixed layout. I would combine explicit checks for the spatial relationships requested in the prompt with human preferences about how well the overall composition works, while preserving room for different valid interpretations.

sol-6.1.text: I would treat composition as one component of the reward, alongside how well the image follows the prompt and its visual quality. You want to capture things like the placement of the subject, the balance between foreground and background, and whether the spatial relationships make sense. But you don’t want to reduce that to a rigid rule like, “The subject must always be on a third.” A centered composition may be exactly what the user wants. So the reward should be conditioned on the prompt and allow multiple valid compositions, ideally informed by human preferences rather than a single aesthetic score.
